scenes.name: San Francisco: Acid Tests y Haight-Ashbury
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: A principios de 1966 había distritos psicodélicos con locales, grupos, ropa, impresos y drogas propios en Londres, Los Ángeles y San Francisco. Los Merry Pranksters de Ken Kesey convirtieron su desafío «Can You Pass the Acid Test?» en fiestas de luces, cine y sonido grabado y devuelto al instante: la segunda, en San José en diciembre de 1965 tras un concierto de los Stones, y nueve más en los tres primeros meses de 1966 (cinco en Los Ángeles, una en Watts). Los beats se habían mudado de North Beach a Haight-Ashbury; los Thelin abrieron la Psychedelic Shop y con Stewart Brand se hizo el Trips Festival (6.000 personas). La banda sonora era Rubber Soul. El caos sustituía al cuidado de Leary por el «set and setting»: en el Acid Test de Watts, Ken Babbs amplificó por micrófono los gritos de una chica en pleno mal viaje.

scenes.name: Alicia, la locura y el regreso a la infancia
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Al final de 1966 el LSD llevó al pop de vuelta a la infancia y a la locura. Los Beatles empezaron el 24 de noviembre «Strawberry Fields Forever», un viaje de Lennon hacia abajo, no hacia atrás, al orfanato junto a su casa, «psicoanálisis con música», unida por Geoff Emerick a partir de dos tomas; luego «When I’m Sixty-Four» y «Penny Lane». En Navidad la BBC aplazó el Alice in Wonderland de Jonathan Miller, sin cabezas de animal, con el sitar de Ravi Shankar y rodado en un hospital militar de víctimas de neurosis de guerra: un catálogo de psicosis. Grace Slick llevó «White Rabbit» a Jefferson Airplane; Syd Barrett escribía sobre el mundo de Lewis Carroll. Proliferaban los discos sobre la locura («They’re Coming to Take Me Away, Ha-Haaa!», «Pandora’s Golden Heebie Jeebies» de los Association), y en el corazón secreto del año, la tristeza frágil de «How Can We Hang On to a Dream» de Tim Hardin.

podcast.title: Discomfort with Commercial Success (1975)
podcast.body: Following the hit "Miracles" and the commercial success of *Red Octopus*, she expressed discomfort, stating, "when miracles hit it was all of a sudden better stick with that shit but I felt odd doing it like I was wearing a costume a monkey suit or something." This highlights her internal struggle with the band's shift from counterculture to pop. "Grace licks said when miracles hit it was all of a sudden better stick with that shit but I felt odd doing it like I was wearing a costume a monkey suit or something."

podcast.title: Backed by Pointer Sisters (Early-Mid 70s)
podcast.body: The Pointer Sisters provided backing vocals for Grace Slick's solo album in the early to mid-70s, showcasing their versatility and demand. "In the early to mid 70s, the sisters backed up recordings by Bashaggs, Sylvester, Betty Davis, and on this recording, the solo album by Jefferson Airplane slash Jefferson Starship front woman Grace Slick."

podcast.title: Decline in the 1970s
podcast.body: Despite her prominence in the late 1960s with Jefferson Airplane, the 1970s saw a decline in her musical force, possibly due to alcohol and drug abuse. She went from lead vocalist to being largely relegated to harmonies and "oh babies" in Jefferson Starship's 70s music. "But the 70s seemed to just swallow Grace Slick or maybe it was the alcohol in the drugs."

podcast.title: Departure from Jefferson Starship
podcast.body: Grace was "essentially kicked out" of the revamped version of the band she formed with Paul Cantner, Jefferson Starship, during the 1970s. "And then she went to essentially being kicked out of the revamped version of the band that she formed with Paul Cantner, Jefferson Starship in the 70s."

podcast.title: Outspoken Personality
podcast.body: Grace Slick maintained her "edge and her outspoken personality" throughout her career, even as her musical prominence waned in the 1970s. "Grace never lost her edge and her outspoken personality, but she was not exactly a musical force of the 1970s."

podcast.title: Peer of Janis Joplin
podcast.body: Grace Slick was considered a contemporary and peer of Janis Joplin, often referred to as a "rock goddess" of the era. "If anyone could have possibly taken hold of the reins, dropped by Janice's death, it was Grace Slick. She was one of Janice's peers and she was a rock goddess."

podcast.title: Survival Through Drug Use
podcast.body: She was mentioned in the context of baby boomers navigating their 30s and changing lifestyles, specifically noting her survival through "doing lots of drugs." "especially if they manage to survive a wider no drag races and doing lots of drugs and I'm just talking about Grace Slick."
